emailSubject: FMB News | US Formally Requests Extradition of Apollo Quiboloy; DFA Transmits Demand to DOJ | August 7, 2026 | 12:00 AM PHT
headline: US Formally Requests Extradition of Apollo Quiboloy; DFA Sends Request to DOJ
kicker: Justice · Extradition · Philippines and United States
deck: The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed receiving the formal US request for Apollo Quiboloy’s extradition and forwarded it to the Department of Justice for evaluation.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The United States formally requested the extradition of detained Kingdom of Jesus Christ founder Apollo Quiboloy to face criminal charges in California. On August 6, the Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed receiving the request from the US State Department and transmitting it to the Department of Justice, the Philippine central authority for extradition.

sections.heading: What we know
paragraphs: DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel confirmed that the extradition papers were received and endorsed to the DOJ for evaluation and possible judicial action.

Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez said US authorities wanted the request handled as soon as possible. A 2021 federal indictment in California charges Quiboloy and several associates with offenses that include sex trafficking of children, labor trafficking, visa fraud, bulk cash smuggling, and money laundering.

Quiboloy was arrested by Philippine authorities in September 2024 and remains in Philippine custody while facing separate domestic cases, including qualified human trafficking and child-abuse charges.
The accusations remain allegations unless proven in court. Quiboloy has denied wrongdoing, and his legal team said it could not comment on the extradition request before receiving formal notice.

sections.heading: Background
paragraphs: The Philippines and the United States are parties to a bilateral extradition treaty signed in 1994. The treaty and Philippine extradition law require the DOJ to assess the request before prosecutors may ask a Philippine court to approve extradition.

The treaty also contains a temporary-surrender mechanism that may apply when a requested person is already facing proceedings in the requested country. Whether that mechanism can or should be used in this case will be determined through the Philippine legal process.

sections.heading: What remains unclear
paragraphs: It remains unclear when the DOJ will complete its assessment, whether prosecutors will seek temporary surrender while Quiboloy’s Philippine cases remain pending, and what objections his defense may raise once formally notified.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: The case tests how Philippine courts balance domestic criminal proceedings, treaty obligations, national jurisdiction, and the interests of alleged victims in two countries. Extradition is a judicial process, not an automatic transfer ordered by either government.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: The DOJ will review the request and supporting documents. If the legal requirements are met, prosecutors may file an extradition petition before a Philippine Regional Trial Court, where Quiboloy’s counsel can contest the request.
